_doc: T-3645: the 1812 tales (data/tales/1812.json, 'Tell me a story') retold for younger readers. Keyed by tale id; each age a list of paragraphs, one for each of the tale's own, in the teller's own voice. Most tales already read at 8-10 and need nothing here. Only the younger ages are written, and the tale itself is never rewritten; no fact enters that the tale does not hold.

8-10: Every few summers I go west to the Rock River to trade with the Sauk. They have horses from the far plains. They have lead from the mines near the Mississippi. We have goods from the traders here at the lake. One of their war leaders is a hard man called Black Hawk. He hates the Americans almost as much as Main Poc does.

He told me the Americans took the Sauk land by the Mississippi with a treaty. His people never said yes to it. The men who signed it were drunk and had no right to sign. He says he will never forgive it. I believe him. I have never met a man who kept a grudge so carefully. He keeps it like a hot coal kept alive in a shell. One day, I think, that coal will set the prairie on fire.

I came down from Milwaukee three days ago. Twenty of us walked the trail along the lake shore. At every creek we met others going the same way. They came from the north and the west. Whole families walked with their horses and dogs and kettles. Everyone was walking to Chicago.

It was as if the whole land was moving, like birds before a storm. Nobody told us to come. We came because everybody was coming. I think that is how big things happen. A chief does not say so. Everybody just starts walking the same way at once, and nobody can stop.

Everyone in this camp knows the name Wells. Twenty years ago the Americans' armies came into our land. Wells was a scout for them. He knew where our villages were and how we fought. He knew because he had been one of the Miami himself. Many of our people died because of what he knew.

So when he rode in yesterday with his Miami, some of the young men spat on the ground. Some of the older men nodded to him. They remember him from before. Back then he was married to Little Turtle's daughter, and he fought against the Americans. A man with two lives has two kinds of enemies. Wells has more than anyone.

Before the traders brought ribbon, my grandma made everything pretty with porcupine quills. You make them soft in your mouth. You flatten them with your teeth. You dye them with roots and berries. Then you sew them down in patterns so fine you would think they were painted.

I still sew quills on moccasins for my family. It takes ten times as long as ribbon. My daughter says, why bother? The trader has ribbon in every color. I tell her this. Your grandma's hands taught mine, and mine will teach yours. When you sew quills, you are holding her hands. She rolls her eyes. One day she will understand.

Last fall I went south with the young men to the Prophet's town on the Wabash River. The Prophet was Tecumseh's brother. He said we must give up the white men's goods and their whiskey. He said we must live like our grandfathers did. If we were strong, he said, the Americans would go back over the mountains.

Before dawn on a cold day in November, we attacked the army General Harrison had brought to the town. I will not tell you about the fighting. When the sun came up, we had lost. The Americans burned the town. The Prophet's magic had not stopped their bullets. Some men stopped believing in him that day. Some men only hated the Americans more. I was one of those.

Every summer the British at Amherstburg give presents to every nation that comes. Amherstburg is down the river from Detroit. They give blankets, kettles, guns, powder, silver, ribbons and red paint. They call us their children and call the king our father. They feast us for days.

The Americans give presents too, at their treaties. But it is never the same. The Americans want land. So far, the British only want friends. I am not a fool. I know the British want something too. But think about it. One is a friend who wants nothing yet. One is a neighbor who wants everything. A man picks the friend. Ask Fox Running what the British promised. He just came from them.

In April we heard about the killings at Lee's farm. Every family in the town left home in the dark. Nobody took anything but the children and a blanket. I carried my youngest on my hip and pulled the other by the hand. The soldiers held the gate open with lanterns until the last of us was in.

We have lived in the fort ever since. That is four months, all crowded into the officers' rooms and storerooms with the soldiers' wives. My own house is just over there, a short walk away. The door is shut, and the garden is full of weeds. I can see it from the walls. After tomorrow I will never see it again.

The Kinzies will not march with the soldiers tomorrow. Mrs. Kinzie and the children will go by water, in their own boat. The boatmen and the nurse will go too. They will meet us down the lake. Mr. Kinzie will walk with the soldiers. He says he will not be seen to hide.

People say Mrs. Kinzie was taken when she was a girl. The Senecas took her from Pennsylvania and raised her. She knows the people in the camps better than any officer here. She has said nothing about tomorrow. She just keeps packing in her quiet way. Find her and ask her. One look from her tells you more than a speech from the captain.

Margaret Helm is seventeen. She married the lieutenant last year. She is the most cheerful person in this whole sad fort. Her mom is Mrs. Kinzie. Her real dad was a British officer. So her dad wore the King's coat, and her husband wears the President's.

She can ride, and she can shoot. She has told us all she is not afraid of anything. I think that is mostly true. Tomorrow she will ride with the soldiers instead of going in her mom's boat. She will not leave her husband. Find her and ask her why. She will laugh and tell you, as if it were the easiest thing in the world.

Rebekah Heald came here in 1811 on horseback, all the way from Louisville. She was a bride of twenty. Her husband came, and so did Cicely, who worked for her, and Cicely's baby. She rode the whole way. People say the officers' wives in Detroit would have gone by boat and been carried to shore.

Her uncle is Captain Wells, the scout. She rides like him, low on the horse's neck, and fast. The officers say she is a good shot too. Tomorrow she rides with the soldiers. All afternoon I have seen her check the strap on her saddle twice an hour. She is not as calm as she looks.

Mr. Kinzie made things out of silver before he was a trader. He still makes the silver himself. He makes pins, earrings, arm bands, crosses, and little round pieces with holes for the thread. The Potawatomi sew it on their clothes in rows. A man in his best coat shines like a lake in the sun.

That is how Kinzie built his trade here. He did it with silver that people wanted to wear, not with guns or whiskey, though he sells those too. He knows every chief's name. He knows every chief's wife's name, and their kids' names too. If you want to understand Chicago, find him. He is the town, more than the fort is.

Two months ago, at sunset on 17 June, the gate was being shut. Mr. Kinzie and Jean Lalime met just outside it. Lalime turned Indian words into English for the army. The two men said angry words. Nobody agrees what it was about. Some say the trade. Some say an old fight. Some say Lalime had been writing letters to Fort Wayne about Kinzie.

They fought. When it was over, Kinzie was cut on the neck, and Lalime was dead. A friend took Kinzie to Milwaukee that night, until it was safe to come back. Lalime is buried in front of the Kinzie house, inside a little fence. Kinzie sees the grave from his porch every morning. I do not know how a man can drink his coffee looking at that.

Across from the fort stands the government's store, called the factory. The plan was for the government to sell goods to the Potawatomi at a fair price. It would be cheaper than the British traders. That would make them friends. Mr. Irwin ran it for three years. The whole time, he grumbled that the Indians liked Kinzie's goods better.

He left in July and gave the keys to Doctor Van Voorhis. Now the store is being emptied out to the camps, as the captain promised. Out go cloth, kettles, blankets and paint. The people take them and look at the fort. They do not say thank you. You cannot buy a friend in a week with things you would not sell him for three years.

Jean Baptiste Chandonnai is Mr. Kinzie's clerk. He is the only man in Chicago who is welcome in every house and every lodge. He is French and Potawatomi both, and he is young. He slips between the trading house and the camps like a fish between rocks.

He keeps the books. He turns words from one language to another. He carries messages. This week he has carried lots of messages. Everyone wants to know what everyone else is thinking, and he is the only one who can ask. If you find him, he will greet you kindly. He is very good at greeting people kindly and telling them nothing.

Last winter I was sent with the goods to a trading post on the Kankakee River for the winter. There were two of us, and a Potawatomi family who traded with us. For four months I saw no other white face. The snow came up to the roof of our hut. At night the wolves sat in a ring around it and howled.

When our flour ran out, the family took us in. The old woman gave me moccasins lined with rabbit fur. I wore them until they fell apart. When I came back to Chicago in the spring, I had forgotten how to talk to Americans. I still have not quite remembered.

Mr. Kinzie keeps a house next to his own for us, his hired men. It has bunks, a fire, a table, and a fiddle on the wall that nobody can play well. In the evening we sit there and smoke. We argue about which of us has the worst back.

Tonight nobody is arguing. Everybody is fixing something, or sharpening something, or packing something. Old Baptiste tells the best stories of all of us. He started a story about a werewolf in Quebec. He stopped halfway, and nobody asked him to finish. That never happens.

Listen at dawn tomorrow. You will hear George Burnett's fife before you hear the birds. A fife is a little flute. He has been a soldier since 1806. He can play every tune the army ever wrote, and a few it never did. He plays the wake-up call as if he is mad at the sun for being late.

In the winter, the snow piles up to the fence, and there is nothing to do but fix boots. Then he plays dance tunes in the barracks. The men dance with each other, since there is nobody else to dance with. I once saw a sergeant waltz a corporal around the stove. If you want to hear him, ask nicely. He acts shy. Then he plays until you beg him to stop.

I joined the army at seventeen. A sergeant in Pennsylvania bought me supper and told me about the West. He did not say a word about the mosquitoes. He did not talk about the fevers, or the winters. He did not tell me how the January wind off the lake goes right through a wool coat like paper.

But he did not lie about the West. I have seen buffalo on the far prairie. They looked like a dark smudge moving like a cloud's shadow. I have seen the lake turn green, then gold, then gray, all in one afternoon. If I get home, I will tell my brothers about it. They will not believe a word.

After the killings in April, the captain made soldiers of every grown man in town who was not one already. There are twelve of us. Thomas Burns is our sergeant. He was a soldier himself. When his time was up, he stayed here and married a widow with a house full of kids.

We practice marching on the parade ground with the real soldiers. They laugh at us. We march like farmers going to market, and that is what we are. But every one of us has a family inside these walls. A man fights harder when his own kids are in the wagon behind him. Find Burns. He will tell you we are getting better. That is almost true.

I came here from Detroit as second in charge. I married the trader's stepdaughter. Some of the officers have not forgiven me for being happy. Margaret is the bravest girl in the Northwest. She told me she will ride beside the soldiers tomorrow. I have stopped arguing.

I did not agree with the captain about the march. I told him so once, the proper way. Then I kept quiet, because that is what an officer does. Tomorrow I will march where I am told, and fight if I must. If you see Margaret, do not tell her I am afraid. Tell her I said she rides better than I do. It is true.
